newsitem.title: USA: US insurance firms gain in Japan pact - Barshefsky.
newsitem.headline: US insurance firms gain in Japan pact - Barshefsky.

text.p: The U.S.-Japan insurance agreement announced Sunday would open the major part of the Japanese insurance market to U.S. firms over the next few years, Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said.

Barshefsky, speaking in a telephone conference with reporters after returning from Japan, said the measures would give foreign firms access to so-called "primary" sector, which includes life, property and casualty insurance, by 1998.

Large Japanese firms, which dominate the primary sector, would not be allowed into the so-called "third" sector, where some foreign firms already have a presence, until 2-1/2 years after the primary sector reforms are in place, she said.
The third sector includes specialty coverage, such as cancer, travel and accident insurance.
"We have important elements of primary sector dereg(ulation) in exchange for very limited entry into the third sector," Barshefsky said.
She declined to say how much the deal would mean to U.S. companies, but said there was "no question" U.S. firms would be competitive.
Sunday's agreement followed 14 months of wrangling over implementation of an insurance pact the two countries signed in 1994.
Barshefsky said the new agreement was complementary to, and did not replace, the 1994 accord.
"This is exactly, exactly, what was envisioned in the '94 agreement," she said.
Japan has the world's second-largest insurance market, with annual premiums of $341 billion. Foreign firms have a market share of less than four percent, Barshefsky said.
She indicated that negotiations had been tough, but declined to say what consequences the United States had threatened in the event of failure of the talks.
"The Japanese government fully understood the seriousness which the U.S. government attached to the insurance talks," she said. "All the cards were on the table."

She said Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka adopted a pragmatic approach, in part because insurance reform was consistent with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's financial sector deregulation slated for 2001.
"There's no question that a very pragmatic attitide took hold, in part spurred by Japan's own professed need to deregulate, and spurred by very insistent U.S. action," she said.
"We've been at this for 14 months and we simply would not give way. We knew what we wanted, we knew what the 1994 agreement called for and we were not going to give way," she said.
Barshefsky said she was in Tokyo when President Bill Clinton announced her nomination as permanent Trade Representative. She has been Acting Trade Representative since April.
She said it was very early in the morning Tokyo time when the announcement was made, and she was unable to stay awake to watch a live television broadcast.
"I honestly did try to stay up, but I just couldn't do it," she said.
Barshefsky watched her nomination as Acting Trade Representative in April on an airport television set in Los Angeles as she returned from a trade mission.
